newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs may reject changes to EU procurement law.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs may reject changes to EU procurement law.

text.p: Euro-MPs may reject a draft directive updating European Union laws on public procurement unless the Council of Ministers accepts key changes to the text, a European Parliament official said on Wednesday.

"Given the heated nature of the debate so far, it is possible the parliament could reject the whole directive," the official from the parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee told Reuters.

The parliament is due on May 14 to give a second reading to a European Commission proposal to bring the EU's three procurement directives -- 93/38/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 93/37/EEC -- into line with the new GATT Government Procurement Agreement.

Parliament rejected a first Commission proposal -- COM(55)107 -- last July, saying the Commission had been over-zealous and the planned changes to the existing directives should be scaled down to the minimum required to respect the GPA.

The Commission subsequently produced a new text -- COM(96)598 -- which took on board a number of parliament's requests and was accepted by EU ministers last December but Euro-MPs are still unhappy with the result.
Since parliament's approval of the draft directive is required for it to become law, a clash seems almost inevitable.

Under the GPA, which entered into force on January 1, 1996, the EU and its most important trading partners agreed to widen access to contracts offered by publicly-owned utilities, opening up markets worth an estimated 350 billion Ecus.

Parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee argues that the changes to EU laws proposed by the Commission will put EU suppliers at a disadvantage by binding them to obligations their foreign competitors will not have to fulfil.

Euro-MPs also complain that the Commission proposals will also extend the provisions of the GPA to the so- called "excluded" sectors (energy, water, transport and telecommunications), which ought not to be covered, and to private as well as public entities.

Parliament is particularly keen for the Commission and Council to remove from the directive a rule preventing contracting entities from seeking technical advice from a commercial firm when drafting the technical specifications of a call for tender.
The Commission has argued that this could give advising firms who have a commercial interest in the procurement a competitive advantage in bidding for the contract.

Parliament is expected next week to say that while it accepts there should be controls to ensure competition is not precluded, the authorities should be able to seek external advice, especially in cases where complex technical problems have to be solved.
The Commission and Council are likely to refuse parliament's demand so a tricky period of negotiations is on the cards, the official said.
If no agreement is reached within the six weeks allowed for conciliation talks, the parliament could well throw the whole proposal out, he said.
